title: Officer hailed as a hero in fatal shooting
article: A Toronto police officer is a hero for fatally shooting a shotgun-toting 63-year-old who was gunned down in an alleyway over the weekend, a police lawyer said yesterday.
Gary Clewley said the officer likely saved the life of his wounded partner, who was shot in the shoulder as police responded to a call involving an emotionally disturbed man.

The armed man "was going to finish off the guy that he'd earlier shot," Mr. Clewley said yesterday after visiting the scene of the shooting on Dufferin Street in west Toronto at 2021 Dufferin St., near Rogers Road.
"That's what I mean about him being a hero -- he saved that guy's life," the lawyer said.
Mr. Clewley said three officers went to an address near Dufferin Street after a female business owner called police around 6:30 p.m. Saturday to report that a man with a gun was threatening her.
"He said that the woman had brought SARS to Canada; that was part of his threat," Mr. Clewley said. "So I mean, right off the top you know you're not dealing with somebody who's got a full deck."
After the officers entered a short, narrow laneway near a shiatsu-massage clinic, the man fired a blast from a shotgun, hitting one of them in the arm, he said.
The injured officer fell and the second one moved out of the way. It left the third officer with a clear shot at the assailant from the end of the laneway, according to Mr. Clewley.
The province's Special Investigation Unit, which probes all shootings and serious injuries involving police officers, is investigating the incident.
It won't comment on its findings so far, but is processing forensic evidence at its Mississauga headquarters.
The SIU refused to name the dead man, saying his family asked that his identity be withheld.
But CFTO News reported yesterday that the dead man was Antonio Bellham, a neighbourhood resident who was said to have had an extensive gun collection.
Mr. Clewley, a lawyer who frequently defends police against allegations of wrongdoing, said he doubts the SIU will find anything wrong with the officers' conduct.

"When their conduct is scrutinized, they're going to find they did nothing but potentially sacrifice themselves for this storeowner who was being blamed by a lunatic for something she didn't do," Mr. Clewley said.

CFTO also identified the wounded officer as Sergeant Al Jenkins. Mr. Clewley said it is too soon to tell whether the injured officer will get the full use of his arm back or whether he will be permanently disabled.
The SIU typically investigates between 150 and 250 cases of death or injury involving police every year. However, firearms deaths are rare, accounting for only one to five investigations each year.
In the overwhelming majority of cases, SIU investigators find no fault with the conduct of the officers.
Between four and nine officers have been charged yearly for the past five years, a small percentage of the total number of police officers who fell under scrutiny.
And even if charges are brought, juries can disagree with the SIU's findings.

In 2000, four Toronto police officers responded to a call about an emotionally disturbed person at a 7-Eleven convenience store. Though manslaughter charges were brought against the officers, a jury exonerated them this past fall.
